newsitem.title: UK: Euro Products Outlook - bearish pressure looms.
newsitem.headline: Euro Products Outlook - bearish pressure looms.

text.p: European oil product markets look under pressure with the usual seasonal leader, gasoline failing to deliver despite Mediterranean tightness.
Some of fuel oil's strength last week could be shed as heavy short-covering moderates and after gas oil's weaker IPE open on Monday in line with sharp crude falls on Friday.
Gasoline prices in northwest Europe need to fall in comparison to U.S. numbers before profitable transatlantic arbitrage opportunities open up again.
"The market is well and truly closed," said one dealer, before NYMEX futures plunged lower again on Friday.
But if U.S. outlets look closed, there may be some help available in the Med, which is gasping for gasoline.

"The situation is a little bit stressed in Italy at the moment," one refiner said. Outstanding prompt requirements for mixed leaded/unleaded cargoes are unfilled and dealers wonder where the gasoline is going to come from. "I only see availabilities in the region out towards the end of the month," one trader said.
But even northwest Europe may not be able to provide much help - shipping is scarce, and expensive, at the moment.
Naphtha is looking undervalued against crude and petrochemical demand in Europe is expected to be good, considering high prices for petchems and naphtha in Asia.
Gas oil was tipped to move sideways to lower with the current low demand, good supply situation unlikely to change.
They said the contango on benchmark IPE gas oil was encouraging some players to put wintergrade low sulphur diesel material into storage. This may stem recent falls.
At least three Algerian cargoes and two flexi-cargoes out of Milford Haven were set to go into storage ARA and Le Havre while Libyan and Algerian material was going into storage in Lavera and Rouen.
Traders said the hoarding of low sulphur might help firm prices but others said that while Russia kept pumping out material, the market would remain well-supplied.

"You'd think the fact that the whole of Europe has converted to 0.05 use would make for more demand and a better market," said one trader. "But last year when everyone did their calculations no one accounted for Russian supply."
"They're producing lots of it and it's good stuff," he said.
High sulphur fuel enjoyed a surge last week to hit levels unseen for around two months but traders were unsure how long the run would continue.
If bunker demand weakens, values could fall away from their $87/$88 levels towards the mid-$80s but a continued scarcity of Russian cracked cargoes would counteract this.

One percent markets will continue to trade sporadically. They resisted much of the effect of crude's fall last week, partly because high sulphur barges were so high, and should stay in the $92-$95 fob range, dealers said.
In the Med supply was tight last week and dealers saw scant relief ahead, with Russian cargo schedules light and arbitrage sucking material to Asia.
"There are very thin Russian loading programmes," said one Med watcher. He doubted if the traders who pushed numbers down last week could repeat the trick.
